paragraphs: Rava son of Rav Avya the Elder, to Rav Ashi, Menahot. Go and examine: you will not find in Menahot or anywhere in the Talmud that Rav Avya the Elder had a son named Rava. We do, however, find Rav Aha son of Rav Avya the Elder speaking to Rav Ashi more than ten times (see there), and repeatedly challenging Rav Ashi (see there). At the beginning of my study I thought that perhaps Yuhasin derived this from Menahot 37b: R' Avya son of Rav Avya used to place tefillin opposite his heart; Rav Ashi sat before Amemar, etc. Yuhasin would have been troubled that nowhere in the Talmud do we find Rav Avya son of Rav Avya, and therefore supposed that one should emend to Rava son of Rav Avya. Since just afterward Rav Ashi is mentioned as sitting, he accordingly wrote ‘Rava son of Rav Avya said to Rav Ashi, Menahot.’ Recently the new Talmud editions with the glosses of the eminent R' Shmuel were printed, correcting it to Rav Aha bar Rav Avya the Elder, which pleased me. But I shall tell you, recorded in truthful writing, the origin of his error. First I shall copy Yuhasin's words under aleph: ‘Rav Avya the Elder, who is a great man; so too Rabbah bar Rav Huna to Rava his son.’ End quotation. What discerning person could understand this? The Lord enlightened my eyes to understand his intent and the origin of his error. I shall copy the Gemara, Hullin 124b: Rav Avya the Elder asked Rabbah bar Rav Huna about a sealed thighbone, etc. He replied, ‘A raven flies’ (look at a raven flying in the air; that is, he diverted him to another matter—Rashi). Rava his son said to him, ‘Is this not Rav Avya the Elder of Pumbedita, whom the master praises to us as a great man?’ He answered, ‘Today, “Support me with cakes”’ (I need strengthening, for my strength was exhausted by the exposition I delivered today, since it was a festival-season Shabbat—Rashi), ‘and he asked me something requiring reasoning.’ End quotation. The Arukh, entry סמך, writes: that day they supported him in the academy and seated him at its head. End quotation. This needs examination: how could Rav Avya, who was already old when he asked Rav Huna—as it says, ‘Rav Avya the Elder asked Rav Huna’—and Rav Huna is known to have presided forty years, ask Rav Huna's son Rabbah on the day he was appointed head? Presumably Rabbah bar Rav Huna was not appointed head until his father died. Yuhasin understood ‘Rava his son said to him’ to mean that Rav Avya the Elder's son spoke to Rabbah bar Rav Huna: ‘Is this not Rav Avya the Elder, whom the master praises as a great man?’ On that basis you can understand Yuhasin's words under aleph: ‘Rav Avya the Elder, who is a great man; so too Rabbah bar Rav Huna to Rava his son’—meaning Rava son of Rav Avya the Elder, to whom Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, ‘Today I,’ etc.: yes, he is a great man, and he asked me a question requiring reasoning. Accordingly he wrote the present notice, following his understanding there that Rava was Rav Avya the Elder's son. But he erred: ‘Rava his son said to him’ means Rabbah bar Rav Huna's son said to his father Rabbah bar Rav Huna, ‘Does not the master praise Rav Avya the Elder as a great man?’ I shall show you a parallel in Beitzah 21a: Rav Avya the Elder asked Rav Huna about an animal half-owned by a gentile, etc. He answered, ‘A raven flies.’ When he left—Rav Avya, Rashi explains—Rabbah his son told him—that is, Rav Huna's son spoke to his father, Rashi explains, intending to exclude the interpretation that ‘Rabbah his son’ means Rav Avya's son—‘Is this not Rav Avya the Elder, whom the master praises as a great man?’ (Why did you put him off, so that he left humiliated?—Rashi.) He answered, ‘What shall I do for him? Today, “Support me with cakes”’ (it is a festival; I expounded publicly and became ill from the exertion. I apply to myself ‘Support me with cakes’: bring me a meal and let me eat—Rashi), ‘and he asked me a question requiring reasoning.’ End quotation. At the beginning of my study I thought to reconcile Hullin with Beitzah by emending Hullin to ‘Rav Avya asked Rav Huna,’ etc.; ‘he said, “A raven,”’ etc.; ‘Rabbah his son said, “Is this not,”’ etc. Thus ‘Rava his son’ would be a scribal error for Rabbah; Rav Avya would twice have asked Rav Huna, and each time Rabbah his son would have asked, ‘But does not the master,’ etc. Yet this is not right: once he had answered his son that the exertion of expounding caused him to put off Rav Avya the Elder and divert him, a wise son would not have asked a second time. I also saw several places in the Talmud where Rabbah bar Rav Huna had a son named Rava (see shortly). Therefore no emendation is needed. There were two episodes: once Rav Avya asked Rav Huna, who put him off with ‘A raven flies,’ and Rabbah son of Rav Huna asked him, ‘Is this not,’ etc. The second time Rav Avya asked Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who likewise put him off as his father had, saying ‘A raven flies.’ His son Rava asked, ‘Does not the master praise,’ etc.; he answered his son as his father Rav Huna had answered him: ‘Today I,’ etc. Be that as it may, Yuhasin erred by including Rava bar Rav Avya the Elder. His statement ‘Rava bar Rav Avya to Rav Ashi, Menahot’ may nevertheless have arisen as I first wrote: having understood that Rav Avya had a son named Rava, he emended ‘Rav Avya bar Rav Avya’ in Menahot to Rava bar Rav Avya. Understand this. But the new Talmud editions' reading Rav Aha is more appropriate, since an error from Aha to Avya could readily occur.
